title: Area 51 and the Nevada ranges
notes: The documented history of the site (U-2, OXCART, Tacit Blue) beside the claims made about it.

lead.text: Area 51 at Groom Lake is a real CIA and Air Force test site whose founding the CIA's own history documents, and which presidents have exempted from environmental disclosure every year since 1995. Around that documented core sit allegations that recovered craft were held on or near the Nevada ranges, made by people such as Bob Lazar and, at second hand, a former EG&G manager.

summary.text: The documented history: the CIA's Richard Bissell chose the Groom Lake site in April 1955 for the U-2, the Atomic Energy Commission added the strip known as Area 51 to the Nevada Test Site at his request, and the programmes that followed, from the U-2 to the Northrop TACIT BLUE stealth demonstrator, are recorded in the Agency's history and in Air Force fact sheets.

The legal shell: annual presidential determinations since 1995 exempt the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake from environmental disclosure, and a workers' suit over the site was dismissed on state secrets and statutory exemption grounds.

The contractors: EG&G is described as the classified site services contractor for the Nevada complex in the testing era, and DOE records name Bechtel Nevada and then a Northrop Grumman-led consortium as management and operating contractors of the Nevada Test Site.

The allegations: Lazar's S-4 account is sited by reference to Groom Lake, Edgar Fouche narrated Groom Lake work and a TR-3B based at Papoose, and George Knapp relays an EG&G manager's statement about a recovered saucer. On the board's reading, the site's long official silence shows how a contractor-staffed installation can be kept off the acknowledged record, which is an inference, not a document.

record.text: The CIA history records that Allen Dulles gave Bissell charge of the U-2 project on 26 November 1954, and that on 12 April 1955 Bissell, Col. Osmund Ritland, Kelly Johnson and Lockheed's chief test pilot Tony LeVier flew over Nevada and spotted an airstrip by the salt flat known as Groom Lake, near the northeast corner of the AEC's Nevada Proving Ground.

The same history records that Bissell and Miller asked the Atomic Energy Commission to add the Groom Lake area to its Nevada holdings, that AEC Chairman Lewis Strauss agreed, and that President Eisenhower approved adding the strip known by its map designation as Area 51 to the Nevada Test Site.

The history was written by the CIA History Staff in 1992 and released on 25 June 2013 with its Area 51 references intact. It states that the Agency's manned overhead reconnaissance programme ran twenty years, from late 1954 to 1974, and names the record sets it was built from.

It also records that Blue Book investigators regularly checked UFO reports against U-2 flight logs with the Agency's project staff, which let them eliminate the majority of reports, although they could not reveal the true cause to the people who wrote in.

Presidential determinations exempting the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake from federal environmental disclosure requirements have been published in the Federal Register every year since 1995; they never name the facility or describe its contents.
In Kasza v. Browner the Ninth Circuit in 1998 upheld the dismissal of claims arising from the Groom Lake facility on state secrets and statutory exemption grounds, and certiorari was denied.

An Air Force fact sheet records that the USAF, DARPA and Northrop worked together from 1978 to 1985 on TACIT BLUE to show that curved surfaces give a low radar return; it first flew in February 1982, flew 135 times, and went on museum display in May 1996.

DOE technical reports name Bechtel Nevada as the Nevada Test Site's research organisation of record through 2006, succeeded by National Security Technologies, a Northrop Grumman-led consortium. The site is DOE and NNSA property operated by contract.

An AF Form 77a of 24 August 1979, from Fouche's own published compilation, records that he was on temporary duty to AFFTC Detachment 3, Nellis AF Range, from 1 June to 14 August 1979. It does not say what he did there: it refers that to a separate report which is not in the collection.

The Las Vegas Review-Journal of 21 August 1990 described Lazar's claim, as of that date, as being that the government was testing alien spacecraft at the Nevada Test Site, a Department of Energy site, rather than on the Air Force range where the account later settled.

claimed.text: George Knapp reports that Alfred O'Donnell, whom he describes as the first general manager of EG&G in Nevada, told him that they had a flying saucer recovered from New Mexico and a live being with it. Knapp named O'Donnell to Congress in September 2025; the account reaches the public only through Knapp.

Knapp also states that O'Donnell recorded a deathbed confession to be released after his death; no recording has appeared, which the board notes fits either suppression or a recording that does not exist.

Jake Barber said on a 2025 podcast that an unnamed senior EG&G engineer told his great uncle about an egg-shaped craft the size of an SUV whose hull the team could not penetrate. The account is third-hand: engineer to great uncle to Barber.

Bob Lazar sites his claimed S-4 facility on the Nellis range about fifteen miles south of Area 51 at Groom Lake and says he was bussed there from Groom. The claim anchors itself to a documented facility; that does not transfer the facility's documentation to the claim.

Edgar Fouche's 1998 presentation narrates Groom Lake work at length, which the board holds at Tier 2 on his word alone, and passes on a friend's sighting of a TR-3B based at Papoose; he does not claim to have seen it himself.

The Wilson-Davis notes record Wilson describing a 1997 attempt to gain access to a special access programme holding recovered material in contractor custody. A later report places the meeting at an EG&G facility in Las Vegas, which the board holds at Tier 3.

Knapp attributes to the Senate investigator Richard D'Amato a private view that a cover-up inside a private company such as Lockheed Martin, EG&G or Northrop Grumman was entirely feasible; D'Amato did not say this on the record, and the board carries it at Tier 3.

A researcher known as UAP Gerb said on a 2025 podcast that retrieval teams in two witness accounts were likely DOE nuclear emergency search teams helped by contractors like EG&G; he framed this as his own inference from the witnesses' descriptions.

contested.text: D'Amato's own public statement is that his preliminary Senate inquiry into 1940s crash allegations did not appear to merit further investigation. The inquiry reached EG&G and stopped: at a meeting Knapp arranged, O'Donnell said nothing.

Aerial photographs of Papoose Lake show nothing on the lakebed and no access road, and Tom Mahood and T.D. Barnes, by unrelated routes, both say the designator S-4 belongs to a radar facility on the Tonopah side of the range rather than to anything at Papoose Lake.

Peter Merlin, a historian of Area 51 since 1984, says he has always been extremely skeptical of Fouche: the photograph Fouche captioned as HAVE BLUE is the first YF-117A prototype, no Steve Stenson ever commanded AFFTC, and the KGB props are fakes available in surplus stores.

The letter Fouche calls a SAC-DARPA classified document carries no classification marking and is signed by a technical sergeant in a personnel assignments section; its redactions were applied by Fouche himself, and the compilation as a whole shows an ordinary avionics maintenance career.

The real black-programme aircraft of the period does not match the TR-3B: TACIT BLUE is curved, 48 feet across and was retired in 1985, against a claimed triangle of 200 to 600 feet first flown in the early 1990s. No source was found arguing the two were confused.

T.D. Barnes said in 2026 that the CIA's Area 51 records went to Norton Air Force Base and were lost there. The Agency's published history contains no Norton Air Force Base, every Norton in it being a Navy official, and it states it was built from CIA record sets and classified interviews.

The accounts disagree among themselves: in the same 2025 episode whose narration centres EG&G, Greg Rogers ruled EG&G out as owner of the craft he describes and named firms such as Lockheed, Northrop, Boeing or Raytheon instead.
The story of a February 1954 Eisenhower meeting at Muroc, the base later called Edwards, has no primary record and the board carries it as folklore.

questions: Where did TACIT BLUE actually fly from? The fact sheet the board holds names no airfield.
Is there a primary Air Force record, rather than a historian's reference work, identifying AFFTC Detachment 3 with Groom Lake, and where is the separate report on Fouche's duties there?
What were O'Donnell's exact title and dates at EG&G Nevada, and does the deathbed recording Knapp describes exist anywhere?
Does any written product of D'Amato's Senate inquiry survive, and which committee chairman asked for it?
Does any government document use the designator S-4, and did anything ever stand at Papoose Lake at any date?
What records underlie EG&G's classified site services role at Groom Lake, beyond the worker litigation and the presidential determinations?
Why do the claimed accounts disagree on which contractor held the material, EG&G or an airframe prime?
